title: Learning Permutation from Structure Without Supervision
topic: General Machine Learning->Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Learning
claim: Uniform global sharpening forces all assignments to discretize together; locally adaptive control fixes confident ones while keeping ambiguous ones flexible.
layout: 4 columns left-to-right, adaptive row above global row, color-coded highlighted tiles
description: A four-stage left-to-right figure. At the left is a scrambled 3x3 face image with one pink-outlined ambiguous tile and one green-outlined confident tile. Dashed gray arrows link those tiles to rows in the adaptive beta heatmap. The second column stacks two beta heatmaps. The top one, Adaptive beta, is a varied blue-to-red grid. The bottom one, Global beta, is uniformly blue. A colorbar runs from High beta (discrete) to Low beta (diffuse). The third column shows the matching soft permutation matrices P in grayscale. Adaptive P has soft, blurry rows at the ambiguous positions and sharp ones elsewhere. Global P is a crisp diagonal throughout. The fourth column shows the Adaptive and Global reassembled faces, with the pink and green tiles outlined to show where the two differ. A legend at lower left defines the colors. The eye goes first to the colorful adaptive heatmap.
caption: Overview of entropy-adaptive inverse-temperature control for learning permutations with Gumbel–Sinkhorn. Starting from a scrambled input image (left), the model predicts a soft permutation over tile positions. The adaptive inverse-temperature field β varies across rows and columns based on assignment uncertainty, assigning high β to confident tiles while keeping ambiguous tiles diffuse. In contrast, a single global β applies uniform sharpening to all assignments. The resulting soft permutation matrices P . Adaptive temperature yields a mixture of sharp and soft rows, whereas global temperature forces all rows to discretize uniformly. Final reassemblies obtained by decoding the soft permutations. Adaptive temperature preserves flexibility in ambiguous regions while correctly fixing confident tiles, thereby improving reconstruction quality.
abstract: Many learning problems require uncovering a hidden ordering that reveals structure in unordered data, such as monotonicity in sorting or spatial continuity in jigsaw reconstruction. In these settings, permutations can be learned as latent operators by optimizing objectives defined directly on the reordered output, often without access to ground-truth orderings. Differentiable relaxations such as Gumbel-Sinkhorn make this approach practical by approximating permutation matrices with doubly stochastic matrices. However, learning from structure without supervision induces a non-uniform uncertainty: some assignments become confident early, while others remain ambiguous. Existing methods control this process using a single global temperature, forcing all assignments to sharpen or diffuse simultaneously and leading to instability at scale. We introduce an entropy-adaptive formulation of Gumbel-Sinkhorn that locally modulates temperature based on assignment uncertainty. This allows confident assignments to discretize early while preserving exploration where uncertainty remains. Across sorting and jigsaw reconstruction tasks and in routing-style settings, adaptive entropy control improves training stability and final permutation quality relative to fixed-temperature baselines, particularly as problem size and assignment ambiguity increase.
